t: Minimum Time to Make Array Sum At Most x — Knapsack on Operation Order
o: Each second ALL elements grow by nums2[i], then we may zero ONE element. If we perform t operations total, element i zeroed at time τ_i ends at value nums1[i] + nums2[i]·t − (nums1[i] + nums2[i]·τ_i) = nums2[i]·(t − τ_i) if zeroed, else nums1[i] + nums2[i]·t. Final sum = t·Σnums2 + Σnums1 − Σ over operated i of (nums1[i] + nums2[i]·τ_i). So maximizing the total 'saving' via a knapsack where assigning item i as the j-th operation saves nums1[i] + nums2[i]·j. Sorting by nums2 descending makes taking the largest multipliers with largest growth rates optimal. Example 1 achieves sum 4 at t=3.
k: Final sum decomposes into baseline growth minus savings nums1[i]+nums2[i]·τ_i; maximize savings with a knapsack over (item, operation rank).

a.i: Sort indices by nums2 descending. dp[j] = max saving using j operations among the first m items. After processing each prefix of size m, check whether any t ≤ m satisfies sum1 + t·sum2 − dp[t] ≤ x; the first such t is the answer since feasibility is monotone in t (more time only helps).
s: Sort pairs by nums2 descending; compute sum1, sum2.
dp[0]=0, others −∞; iterate items, updating dp[j] = max(dp[j], dp[j−1] + nums1[i] + nums2[i]·j) descending j.
After each prefix, test all t: if sum1 + t·sum2 − dp[t] ≤ x return t.
a.t: O(n²) — knapsack over n items and n ranks, plus O(n log n) sorting

w: The decomposition of the final sum into baseline + savings is the crux; without it the state space seems unbounded. Pitfall: iterating j downward (0/1 knapsack), using 64-bit arithmetic, and checking feasibility after EVERY prefix (earliest feasible t wins).
